before_record.meaning: Growing emigration, armed émigré groups across the frontier, confiscatory legislation, and foreign protection made émigrés a catalyst of confrontation between Assembly, king, and European rulers.
before_record.stance: The émigrés were politically potent as symbols and pretexts even when their direct military capacity was weak.

The Trier ultimatum briefly removes the immediate émigré pretext for war.
The émigré princes are charged with treason as war agitation shifts toward Austria.

evidence.evidence_summary: Girondin speakers raise the possibility of an alternative assembly if Paris destroys Convention freedom.

Bordeaux’s commercial and political background led to a Popular Commission after 2 June. Reports and calls for collective action from other cities helped overcome hesitation; the commission circulated anti-Montagnard propaganda and sent emissaries urging resistant departments to unite in electing a shadow Convention at Bourges.
Records calls for a Bourges convention and an unrealized departmental army.
Breton and Norman authorities repeat the Bourges proposal, while other cities hesitate to endorse it.
Uses the Bordelais to illustrate republican, property-conscious motives and poor military mobilization.
The Bordelais force marched south rather than toward Paris and encamped only twenty miles up the Garonne, illustrating reluctance to leave home territory.
Bordeaux recruited only about a third of its announced 1,200-man departmental force, illustrating reluctance to fight away from home.

evidence.evidence_summary: The abolition of feudal rights guaranteed to German rulers under the Peace of Westphalia brought uncompensated injury and official hostility. Artois settled at Koblenz, joined by Provence and post-Varennes émigrés, while Condé organized further up the Rhine with foreign subsidies. Their disruptive preparations and arrogance alienated ordinary Rhinelanders, but produced more blame for the Revolution rather than sympathy for it.

French officers departed in their thousands to join royalist émigrés, visibly weakening the army just as foreign revolutionary exiles in France advocated armed liberation. Neither the outgoing Constituent Assembly nor the royal family shared those exiles’ confidence.

before_record.label: French military and political crisis of 1793
before_record.meaning: The sequence of Neerwinden, loss of Belgium and the Rhineland, invasions, sieges, Federalist revolt, and surrender of Toulon amid shrinking French forces. Dumouriez’s real betrayal reinforced suspicions of treason, while the executions of failed commanders such as Custine and Houchard made even patriotic generals fear bold action. Suppression of domestic revolts absorbed much of autumn 1793 and delayed the full effect of national mobilization against foreign enemies.
before_record.stance: The crisis was severe but partly self-created by overconfidence, demobilization after 1792, expanding commitments, and the growth of internal and external enemies.
acceptable_access: French military and political crisis of 1793

evidence.evidence_summary: France adds commitments and enemies while the partition settlement frees opponents for the western front.
Neerwinden, Dumouriez’s defection and loss of the Rhineland reverse the French advance.

Reverses, internal revolt, premature volunteer departure and expanding enemies explain the crisis. Dumouriez’s betrayal reinforced suspicions, and executions of failed generals discouraged bold action even by patriotic commanders.
Much of autumn 1793 was spent suppressing domestic revolt before national resources could be fully directed outward.

before_record.label: Great Britain's entry into war with France
before_record.meaning: The convergence of French occupation of Belgium, opening of the Scheldt, threats to the Dutch settlement, revolutionary propaganda, and Louis XVI's execution in ending British neutrality. France formally declared war on Britain on 1 February 1793, and against the Dutch Republic in the same Convention session.
before_record.stance: The author rejects simple ideological inevitability: Pitt initially expected prolonged peace, while concrete Low Countries interests and the regicide crisis precipitated the break.
